passages.happening: “Remind the believers to submit to rulers and authorities, to be obedient and ready for every good work, to malign no one, and to be peaceable and gentle, showing full consideration to everyone” (verses 1-2).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 2 was about life inside the household. Now Paul looks outward, at how believers live among their neighbours and under their rulers.

The churches on Crete were small groups that met privately in homes and refused to worship the gods of the city. That made them easy to suspect. People wondered what they were hiding. Paul wants them known for the opposite of trouble: respectful toward rulers, ready to do good, never speaking evil of anyone, peaceable, gentle, considerate ‘to everyone’.

Notice how wide that is. ‘Malign no one.’ Not the rulers, not the neighbours who suspect them, not the people who worship other gods. ‘Full consideration to everyone.’ Christians are not to treat outsiders with scorn.

‘Ready for every good work’ is a phrase Paul keeps returning to. The church's best answer to suspicion was not argument. It was a life of doing good in public, so that even its critics could see it.
passages.ot:
God told his people in exile to seek the good of the city they lived in, even a foreign one: “Seek the prosperity of the city to which I have sent you as exiles. Pray to the LORD on its behalf” (Jeremiah 29:7).

Daniel served a foreign king so faithfully that his enemies “could find no charge or corruption, because he was trustworthy” (Daniel 6:4). And the psalms call God's people to live at peace: “Turn away from evil and do good; seek peace and pursue it” (Psalm 34:14).
passages.hard:
Does ‘submit to rulers and authorities’ mean believers must obey any ruler in anything, or support a particular leader or party?

What Paul says is plain: believers are to respect those who govern and be good citizens. What he does not say is that rulers may command anything. The Bible itself sets limits. When the council in Jerusalem forbade the apostles to preach, Peter answered, “We must obey God rather than men” (Acts 5:29).

For centuries passages like this were misused to demand obedience to unjust rulers and to defend tyranny and slavery. That use is wrong, and these notes reject it. The same standard holds for every government.

Christians differ on when disobedience is right. Most hold that believers must refuse a command to do evil, as the apostles did; they differ on whether, and how, to resist an unjust ruler beyond that. The site's notes on Romans 13 set out these views. These notes take no side, and Titus does not tell anyone which party or ruler to support. Paul's words are asked of believers under every government, those they chose and those they did not.
passages.asks: Paul asks believers to be known for gentleness and good works toward everyone. Ask how you speak about people in power, especially those you oppose. Ask whether you malign anyone, in person or online. And ask what good work you could do in your town this week that would show your neighbours what Christ is like.

passages.t: Saved by mercy: the washing of new birth
passages.happening:
Paul gives the reason. “For at one time we too were foolish, disobedient, misled, and enslaved to all sorts of desires and pleasures—living in malice and envy, being hated and hating one another” (verse 3).

“But when the kindness of God our Savior and His love for mankind appeared, He saved us, not by the righteous deeds we had done, but according to His mercy, through the washing of new birth and renewal by the Holy Spirit. This is the Spirit He poured out on us abundantly through Jesus Christ our Savior, so that, having been justified by His grace, we would become heirs with the hope of eternal life” (verses 4-7).

“This saying is trustworthy. And I want you to emphasize these things, so that those who have believed God will take care to devote themselves to good deeds. These things are excellent and profitable for the people” (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
Why be gentle with outsiders? Because ‘at one time we too’ were just like them. Paul does not stand outside the list. Foolish, disobedient, misled, slaves to our desires, ‘hated and hating one another’. That was us. People who remember where they came from are slow to look down on anyone.

Then comes one of the richest sentences in Paul's letters. In Greek, verses 4 to 7 are one long, balanced sentence, and Paul calls it ‘trustworthy’, a saying the church may already have known.

‘The kindness of God our Savior and His love for mankind appeared.’ The Greek word for ‘love for mankind’ gives English the word ‘philanthropy’. Greeks praised it in kings who were generous to their people. Paul says the true generous King is God, and his love appeared in Jesus.

‘He saved us, not by the righteous deeds we had done, but according to His mercy.’ Salvation is not a reward for good people. It is mercy for people who were ‘hated and hating’.

How did God save us? ‘Through the washing of new birth and renewal by the Holy Spirit.’ ‘New birth’ means becoming again, beginning a new life. The same word is used in Matthew 19:28 for the renewal of the whole world at the end. What God will one day do for all things, he has already begun in each believer.

Notice who acts. God our Savior saves. The Holy Spirit renews. Jesus Christ pours out the Spirit. Father, Spirit and Son act together in one rescue, the pattern the church confesses as the Trinity.

And then, good deeds. Not to be saved, but because we have been. That is what is ‘excellent and profitable for the people’.
passages.ot:
God's kindness is his own name: “The LORD, the LORD God, is compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness” (Exodus 34:6). Israel too was told that God's gift was not earned: “It is not because of your righteousness or uprightness of heart that you are going in to possess their land” (Deuteronomy 9:5). “He has not dealt with us according to our sins” (Psalm 103:10).

The washing and the Spirit come from Ezekiel's promise: “I will also sprinkle clean water on you, and you will be clean” (Ezekiel 36:25), and “I will put My Spirit within you and cause you to walk in My statutes” (Ezekiel 36:27). The Spirit ‘poured out … abundantly’ recalls Joel: “I will pour out My Spirit on all people” (Joel 2:28). And David prayed, “Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me” (Psalm 51:10).
passages.hard:
Does ‘the washing of new birth’ mean that baptism saves?

Christians read verse 5 in several ways, and these notes do not choose. Roman Catholic, Eastern Orthodox and Lutheran Christians generally hold that it refers to baptism, and that God truly gives new birth through baptism as his appointed means, though grace and faith remain essential and God is not bound by the rite. Reformed and Presbyterian Christians often read it as baptism understood as a sign and seal of the new birth the Spirit works, joined to the reality but not automatically giving it. Baptists and many other evangelicals read the washing as the Spirit's inward cleansing, described with water pictures, as in Ezekiel 36:25-27, and see baptism as the public sign of what has already happened.

All of these readings agree on what the verse most plainly says: God saved us ‘not by the righteous deeds we had done, but according to His mercy’, and it is the Holy Spirit who makes us new. How baptism relates to that new birth is a real and long-standing difference among faithful churches. The note on Acts 2:37-41 and the doctrine study ‘Baptism and the Lord's Supper’ set out these views more fully.
passages.asks: Paul says, ‘At one time we too were foolish.’ Ask whether you remember what you were before grace found you, and how that changes the way you see others. Ask whether you are still trying to earn what God gives by mercy. And ask what good deed you could devote yourself to, not to be saved, but because you are.

passages.t: Avoid foolish quarrels; warn the divisive person
passages.happening:
“But avoid foolish controversies, genealogies, arguments, and quarrels about the law, because these things are pointless and worthless” (verse 9).

“Reject a divisive man after a first and second admonition, knowing that such a man is corrupt and sinful; he is self-condemned” (verses 10-11).
passages.hearers:
Paul sets two things side by side. Good works are ‘excellent and profitable’ (verse 8). Foolish quarrels are ‘pointless and worthless’ (verse 9). The false teachers on Crete loved long arguments about family trees and fine points of the law. Paul tells Titus not to get drawn in. Some arguments are not worth having.

Then he speaks of ‘a divisive man’. The Greek word is the one that later gave English the word ‘heretic’. But here it describes behaviour more than belief: a person who keeps stirring up quarrels and forming factions, splitting the church into sides.

Notice the patience Paul asks for first. One warning. Then a second. Only after that is Titus to ‘reject’ him, to stop giving him a platform and have nothing more to do with his quarrels. And Paul says such a person is ‘self-condemned’: by refusing every warning, he has shown where he stands.
passages.ot:
Proverbs names the one who stirs up strife among God's people. Among the things the LORD hates is “one who stirs up discord among brothers” (Proverbs 6:19). “Without wood, a fire goes out; without gossip, a conflict ceases” (Proverbs 26:20). “To start a quarrel is to release a flood; so abandon the dispute before it breaks out” (Proverbs 17:14).

And the psalms sing of the opposite: “Behold, how good and pleasant it is when brothers live together in harmony!” (Psalm 133:1).
passages.hard:
Can verse 10, ‘Reject a divisive man’, be used against someone who raises a concern, asks hard questions, or reports harm?

No. Paul is speaking of a person who keeps stirring up quarrels and factions over pointless arguments, and who refuses warning after warning. He is not speaking of someone who tells the truth about wrong that has been done, or asks honest questions. A person who reports abuse is not divisive. The one who did the harm is.

This passage, like others about discipline, has also been badly misused, and that must be faced. Church discipline must never be used to silence someone who has been harmed, to protect someone who has done harm, or to punish someone for asking questions or telling the truth. Abuse and other crimes are reported to the police and the proper authorities, whom Paul calls “God’s servant, an agent of retribution to the wrongdoer” (Romans 13:4). A church meeting is never a substitute for that.

A word to anyone who has been hurt by a church's discipline, or shunned by a church or a family. What happened to you may have been wrong, and it is not wrong to grieve it. Paul's goal was always restoration and comfort, never cruelty or contempt. “The LORD is near to the brokenhearted” (Psalm 34:18). If this still weighs on you, please talk with someone you trust, a pastor, a friend or a counsellor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Paul tells Titus to avoid pointless quarrels. Ask which arguments you keep having that are doing no good to anyone. Ask whether you have ever been the one stirring up sides. And ask whether your church has room for honest questions and hard truths, which are not the same as division.

passages.t: Come to Nicopolis; meet pressing needs
passages.happening:
“As soon as I send Artemas or Tychicus to you, make every effort to come to me at Nicopolis, because I have decided to winter there. Do your best to equip Zenas the lawyer and Apollos, so that they will have everything they need” (verses 12-13).

“And our people must also learn to devote themselves to good works in order to meet the pressing needs of others, so that they will not be unfruitful” (verse 14).

“All who are with me send you greetings. Greet those who love us in the faith. Grace be with all of you” (verse 15).
passages.hearers:
The letter ends, as real letters do, with plans and names.

Paul will send Artemas or Tychicus to take Titus's place, so that the churches are not left without help. Artemas is known only here. Tychicus travelled with Paul and carried his letters to Ephesus and Colossae (Ephesians 6:21; Colossians 4:7).

Then Titus is to come to Nicopolis, where Paul plans to spend the winter, when travel by sea mostly stopped. Several towns were called Nicopolis, ‘city of victory’. Most scholars think Paul meant the one on the western coast of Greece, founded by Augustus to mark his victory at the sea battle of Actium in 31 BC.

Zenas is called ‘the lawyer’. The word could mean an expert in the Jewish law or in Roman law; the text does not say which. Apollos is the gifted teacher from Alexandria who taught in Ephesus and Corinth (Acts 18:24-28; 1 Corinthians 3:6). Travellers in the ancient world depended on friends and churches to supply them for the next part of the road, and Titus is to see that these two have ‘everything they need’.

And one last time, good works. Paul wants believers to ‘meet the pressing needs of others’, real, urgent needs, so that their lives bear fruit. The letter that began with God who cannot lie ends with people who help.
passages.ot: The law told Israel to meet the needs of the poor: “you are not to harden your heart or shut your hand from your poor brother. Instead, you are to open your hand to him” (Deuteronomy 15:7-8). Isaiah described the worship God wants: “to share your bread with the hungry, to bring the poor and homeless into your home” (Isaiah 58:7). And Proverbs says, “Do not withhold good from the deserving when it is within your power to act” (Proverbs 3:27).
passages.asks: Paul ends by asking believers to meet pressing needs. Ask what pressing need is near you right now: a neighbour, a stranger, someone in your church. Ask who is on the road for Christ whom you could help with what they need. And ask whether your life is bearing fruit others can see.
